questions.question: What are blocks and yield in Ruby?
questions.title: Ruby Blocks and Yield
questions.direct_answer: A Ruby block is executable code passed with a method call, written with `{ ... }` or `do ... end`. The receiving method runs it with `yield` and may pass values into it. Blocks power iterators, resource helpers, callbacks, and DSLs. Use `block_given?` when the block is optional; capture it as a `Proc` with `&block` only when you need to store or forward it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand how a method receives and invokes a block, including arguments, return values, closure behavior, and optional blocks.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling `yield` when no block was supplied, or changing `{}` to `do...end` without considering precedence.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the normal block is implicit; `&block` converts it to a `Proc` only when the method must store, inspect, or forward it.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A method call can receive one implicit block written as `{ ... }` or `do ... end`.
`yield(value)` runs the block with `value` and returns the block's result.
`block_given?` tells a method whether the caller supplied a block.
Blocks are closures, so they can read variables from the surrounding scope.
`&block` turns the implicit block into a `Proc` when it must be stored or forwarded.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Ruby block is executable behavior attached to a method call. The caller writes it with `{ ... }` or `do ... end`, and one method call can receive one implicit block. The receiving method owns the stable workflow—such as visiting items or managing a resource—while the block supplies the part that changes for that call.

Inside the method, `yield(value)` pauses the method, runs the attached block with `value`, and returns the block's last expression to the point of the yield. The method may use that result or yield several times. Calling `yield` when no block was supplied raises `LocalJumpError`, so optional block behavior needs `block_given?` or an enumerator return.

Blocks are closures, so they can read local variables from the scope where they were created. In the example, the block uses `factor` even though `transform` does not receive it. When no block is present, `enum_for` returns an Enumerator; calling `each` on that Enumerator later supplies the block and runs the same method workflow.

Use plain `yield` when a method only needs to run its block. A parameter such as `&block` captures that implicit block as a `Proc`, which is useful when it must be stored, forwarded with another `&`, or inspected. Braces bind more tightly than `do ... end`, so use parentheses or split a chained expression when it is not obvious which method owns the block.

sections.title: The method owns the workflow
sections.content:
A block lets a method keep the stable part of an operation and ask the caller for the variable part. `each` owns traversal, `File.open` owns opening and closing a file, and a transaction helper owns commit or rollback. The attached block says what should happen inside that workflow.

The receiving method chooses when to yield, what arguments to pass, and what to do with the returned value.

sections.title: Control moves to the block and back
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Caller
  participant M as Method
  participant B as Block
  C->>M: transform with a block
  M->>B: yield 10
  B-->>M: 20
  M-->>C: Result: 20
```

The block receives `10`, uses any captured values, and returns `20` to the point where the method yielded.

sections.title: Block, yield, and Proc are different roles
sections.content:
| Term | Role | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Block | Behavior attached to a method call | `numbers.map { |n| n * 2 }` |
| `yield` | Runs the implicit block from inside the method | `result = yield(10)` |
| `block_given?` | Checks whether a block exists | `return unless block_given?` |
| `&block` | Captures the block as a `Proc` object | `items.each(&block)` |

sections.title: Build a small block-driven method
sections.content:
```ruby
def transform(value)
  return enum_for(__method__, value) unless block_given?

  result = yield(value)
  "Result: #{result}"
end

factor = 2
puts transform(10) { |number| number * factor }
# Result: 20
```

`factor` comes from the caller's surrounding scope, so the block is a closure. `yield(value)` passes `10` in, the block returns `20`, and the method wraps that result.

sections.title: The precedence trap
sections.content: Braces bind more tightly to the method immediately before them, while `do...end` has lower precedence. In a chained call, `puts numbers.map { |n| n * 2 }` passes the block to `map`, but changing the block form without parentheses can attach it to a different call. Use parentheses or split the expression when ownership is not obvious.

sections.title: Check the control flow
sections.content: In `wrap(5) { |n| n + 1 }`, if `wrap` executes `value = yield(5)`, what is `value`? **6**. The argument travels from `yield` into `n`, and the block's last expression travels back as the result of `yield`.
